[1995] CIA and Guatemala Assassination Proposals, 1952-1954", CIA History Staff Analysis by Gerald K. Haines, June 1995.

CIA records on assassination planning in Guatemala were first gathered pursuant to a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit filed in 1979. All of them were withheld on national security grounds at that time. In 1995, the CIA's historical staff "rediscovered" these records during a search of Guatemala materials to be declassified as part of the agency's "Openness" program. A staff historian, Gerald Haines, was assigned to write this brief history of these operations. He concluded that as early as January 1952, CIA headquarters began compiling lists of individuals in Arbenz's government "to eliminate immediately in event of [a] successful anti-Communist coup." Planning for assassination included budgeting, training programs, creation of hit teams, drafting of target lists of persons, and transfer of armaments. Haines writes that "until the day that Arbenz resigned in June 1954 the option of assassination was still being considered." The CIA, according to this history, did not implement its assassination strategy. But the declassifiers of this study, and other related documents, have deleted the names of the targeted individuals, making it impossible to verify that none of them were killed during or in the aftermath of the coup.

I agree with the conclusion here. Game length does not correlate quality. Though, I think that game length should be correlated with cost. With more games requiring constant internet connection, maybe a system can be implemented where you pay by how long you put into a game, and priced accordingly. I guess that this would burn completionists, maybe the option to purchase the game could still be available. But then developers could be hit in the pocket book when a 7 hour game is released with no replayability. I guess we could receive an influx of cut-scene filler and long loading screens to artificially increase play time, but I guess that's part of the experience.

Length should also be considered the whole entire experience, including all replays.

Portal was short, but I must have replayed it a hundred times. I even bought it for 2 systems.

So while the single run through was short, the life of the game was huge. So is value = Life/Cost the life for Portal was great and the cost was low.

If you want to spread cost across time played, then rent the game, that is essentially what that is.

I have a simple calculation for price to game length. $1/hour of gameplay. This is for how I will play games, and I take into account how much replay I expect to get out of it. So if I think I'll get 10 hours out of a game like The Order: 1886, including with replays, then It's worth $10 to me. So the games I tend to buy at full ($60) price tend to be RPG's. I rarely pay more than $10 for any other type of game.

I've played this, in one sitting. The length was great,except for the ending. There was nice time for experimentation, and through the first half of the game I was able to test out the variety of weapons that they had. The hacking and lockpicking mini games seemed to be designed well, not taking to much time. The "minigames" were well placed and make sense in the story.

The thing that stayed with me, is the story. I really wanted to learn more about these characters and the centuries that they have lived. What happened to all the missing knights? What happened on the last quest for the grail?

Visually this game was stunning, although some of the smoke effects did make it hard to see the men shooting at you. After a few rounds they would have a hazy smoke cloud in front of them that would obscure your line of sight. Level design was good, not great. Each level had there own enemies, whether it was men (heavy shotgunners included), werewolves, or smart werewolves (one on one QTE battle).

They don't mix when you fight, so you never see a battle with werewolves killing everyone in sight, as other men fight them and fight you.

Playing through this game, I felt like I played heavy rain without the holding 3- 4 buttons down to make the "Action" happen. This was much more organic in this regard. I recommend this to people who like story driven games, but note that the ending is unsatisfying (i'm hoping they will add more to this world).

One thing that I somewhat disagree with, or would just like to point out is the comment about the 'rental market'. Full disclosure, I didn't watch the whole thing, so it may have been addressed already.

There really isn't a rental market anymore. It's what, Gamefly, a few games at redbox, and, well, pretty much no-place else, as the B&M rental places have been either disappearing for quite some time, or the ones that still exist don't seem to be investing much money into themselves.

A short / weekend game was great when it cost you 5-8 to rent a game for a week (or slightly less), but not when you're stuck either buying a game, or not.
